  N. [seconds] intent -- narration
keeping the numbering running. Build a real explanatory arc rather than a list of topics. When the explanation is complete, write END on its own line after the last beat.

REQUEST
show eigenvectors as the directions a transformation does not turn, only scales, verify A v equals lambda v numerically, then show a rotation that has no real eigenvectors at all

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [16s] Most directions get knocked off their line -- A transformation, and a fan of vectors pointing every which way. Apply the map and watch what happens to the directions. Almost all of them swing — they come out pointing somewhere new, off the line they started on.
2. [21s] A few come out on the same line -- But not all. Two directions here come out pointing along exactly the line they started on. One is stretched to three times its length, the other to twice. They did not turn at all — the map only scaled them. Those two directions are the eigenvectors, and the scaling factors are the eigenvalues.
3. [20s] Which is exactly what the equation says -- Written down, that is A v equals lambda v: the map applied to the vector gives the same thing as simply scaling the vector. Both sides land on the same point, which the scene checks numerically before claiming it. Finding these directions means asking which vectors the map treats as mere scaling.
4. [30s] Sometimes there are none at all -- And sometimes there are none. Turn the plane by a quarter circle. Every direction without exception comes out pointing somewhere else — there is no line the rotation leaves alone, so there is no real eigenvector to find. Solving for one gives a negative under the square root. That is not a failure of the method; it is the correct answer, and a demonstration that always produces two arrows is drawing something that is not there.
END

REQUEST
show that the determinant is the factor by which a transformation multiplies every area, measure it on an irregular shape as well as the unit square, and explain why a determinant of zero means no inverse

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [15s] Start with a square of area one -- The grid, and the square between the two basis vectors. Its area is one, by definition — that square is the unit the rest of the plane is measured in. Watch what a transformation does to it.
2. [17s] Transform it, and measure what you get -- Apply a map. The square becomes a slanted parallelogram, and measuring it gives an area of five. Not approximately five — exactly, and the same five you get from ad minus bc: three times two, minus one times one.
3. [21s] It is the same factor for every shape -- And it is not special to the square. Take any shape at all — this lopsided quadrilateral, chosen precisely because it is not aligned to anything — and its area is multiplied by the same five. That is what the determinant is: one number saying how much the map stretches every area there is.
4. [28s] Negative means flipped, zero means crushed -- Two cases are worth naming. A negative determinant means the plane was turned over — the area is still scaled, but left and right have swapped. And a determinant of zero means every area became nothing: the whole plane has been crushed onto a single line. Two different points now sit in the same place, so there is no way back. That is why a matrix with zero determinant has no inverse.
END

REQUEST
show that a matrix is a record of where the two basis vectors land, transform the whole grid to match, and explain matrix multiplication as doing one map after another

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [23s] The plane, and the two vectors that describe it -- The whole plane, with its grid. Two special vectors: one step right, and one step up. Every other point is built from those two — a point at one and a half, nought point five, is one and a half of the first plus half of the second. Nothing else is needed to name any point at all.
2. [19s] Move only those two, and everything follows -- Now move them. Send the first to two right and nothing up; send the second to one right and three up. Insist on one thing only: that the grid stays a grid — evenly spaced, parallel lines, origin fixed. That single demand forces where every other point must go.
3. [20s] The matrix is just those two landing places -- Write the two destinations side by side as columns, and that is the matrix. Not a grid of numbers with a rule bolted on — a record of where the two basis vectors went. The multiplication rule everybody learns is only the bookkeeping for rebuilding a point from its two pieces.
4. [22s] Two maps in a row are one map -- And because a map is fully described by where the two vectors land, doing one map and then another is itself just a map — you only need to ask where the two end up after both. That is what multiplying matrices means. Not a rule about rows and columns; a question about where two arrows finish.
END

REQUEST
show two waves travelling in opposite directions, add them point by point to make a standing wave, and work out exactly where the nodes sit and why they never move

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [16s] Two waves, going opposite ways -- Two waves of the same size and the same wavelength, one travelling right and one travelling left. Separately there is nothing remarkable about either. The question is what happens where they overlap, and the answer is simpler than it looks.
2. [23s] At every point, add the two heights -- Here is the rule, and it is all of it. Pick any point along the line. Read the height of the first wave there, read the height of the second, add them. That sum is the height of the combined wave at that point. Do it everywhere and you have the answer — no new physics, just addition.
3. [19s] Some places never move at all -- Watch the combined wave rather than the parts. It is no longer travelling anywhere — it stands still and breathes in place. And certain points never move at all, at any moment. Those are the nodes, and they sit exactly where the two waves are always equal and opposite.
4. [28s] Where the nodes are, and why -- Their positions are not a matter of looking carefully. Adding the two waves algebraically gives twice sine k x, times cosine omega t — and that splits cleanly into a part that depends only on position and a part that depends only on time. The wave is nailed down in space and free to breathe in time. It vanishes wherever sine k x is zero, which is every half wavelength, exactly.
END

REQUEST
show a planet orbiting a star on an ellipse, show that it moves much faster near the star, then shade equal-time wedges at both ends and show they have the same area because nothing twists the orbit

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [22s] One body, one pull, one closed curve -- A star, and a planet falling around it. The only force is a pull towards the centre that weakens with the square of the distance. Nothing steers the planet and nothing keeps it up. The path that comes out of that alone is an ellipse, with the star at one focus rather than the middle.
2. [19s] It is not going round at a steady rate -- Watch it go round. Near the star it tears past; out at the far end it barely moves. The speed swings from nought point eight up to three point zero — nearly four times as fast at one end of the same orbit as at the other.
3. [26s] Equal times sweep equal areas -- Here is the pattern hiding in that. Take the same length of time at the close end and at the far end, and shade the area the line from star to planet sweeps out. Near the star it is a short fat wedge; far away a long thin one. Measure them and they are the same area — not roughly, to within two percent of each other.
4. [26s] Because nothing twists it -- And the reason is almost disappointingly simple. The pull points straight at the star, so it can never twist the planet about the star — and a thing that is never twisted keeps its spin. Distance times sideways speed stays fixed, so halving the distance doubles the speed. The planet does not hurry because it is close. It hurries because it has nothing to slow it down.
END

REQUEST
show convolution as sliding a small window of weights along a signal, and show that the same operation blurs, finds edges, or sharpens depending only on what the three weights are

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [18s] A signal, and a small window of weights -- A signal: sixteen numbers in a row, with two raised patches and some jitter. Below it, a window three wide holding three weights. Slide the window along, and at each position multiply what is underneath by the weights and add. That is the whole operation.
2. [27s] Weights that sum to one: a blur -- Give the window a quarter, a half, a quarter. Every output is a gentle average of a value and its two neighbours, so the jitter flattens while the two patches survive. The weights add to one, which is why the signal does not get brighter or dimmer overall — checked, because a kernel that quietly sums to more than one looks like a blur and is also a gain.
3. [23s] Weights that sum to zero: an edge detector -- Now change nothing but the three numbers. Minus one, zero, plus one. Where the signal is flat, the left and right neighbours cancel and the output is nothing at all. Where the signal steps up or down, they do not cancel and the output spikes. The same sliding sum, and it has stopped smoothing and started finding edges.
4. [24s] Three numbers decide the whole job -- One more: minus a half, two, minus a half. This one exaggerates whatever makes a value differ from its neighbours, so the patches come back with harder edges than they started with. Blur, edge detect, sharpen — one operation, three behaviours, and the only thing that changed was three numbers. That is what a convolutional network learns: not the sliding, the weights.
END

REQUEST
show gradient descent on a stretched valley rather than a bowl, and explain why a single learning rate cannot be both stable across the steep direction and fast along the shallow one

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [19s] A valley, not a bowl -- A loss surface shaped like a valley: steep across, gentle along. The rings are lines of equal loss, and they are stretched — fifteen times more curved in one direction than the other. Real problems look like this. A perfectly round bowl is the case where nothing interesting happens.
2. [22s] A small step is safe, and painfully slow -- Take a step small enough to be safe across the valley. It is safe — every step reduces the loss and the path never wobbles. But look where it goes: straight down the steep walls in a few steps, then a long, patient crawl along the floor, sixty steps later still not at the bottom.
3. [20s] A larger step explodes across the valley -- So take a bigger step. Two and a half times the stable rate. Along the floor that would be a real improvement — but across the valley it overshoots, lands further up the opposite wall than it started, overshoots again, and the loss runs away to something astronomical in thirty steps.
4. [25s] The two demands cannot both be met -- That is the bind. The largest stable step is set by the steepest direction, and the progress you need is set by the shallowest. With curvatures fifteen to one apart, any single number is either too big for one direction or too small for the other. Every optimiser worth its name — momentum, per-parameter rates, Adam — exists to stop using one number for both.
END

END

END

REQUEST
explain the chain rule as two machines feeding into each other, work out the derivative of sine of three x plus one at a point, and show what goes wrong if the outer derivative is taken at the wrong place

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [17s] Two machines, one feeding the other -- Two operations in a row. The first takes x and gives three x plus one. The second takes that answer and gives its sine. Feeding one into the other makes a single function, and the question is how fast that combined function changes.
2. [27s] Push a number through and watch both rates -- Take x equal to nought point four. The inner machine turns it into two point two, and it does so three times as fast as x moves — nudge x by a little and u moves three times that little. Now the outer machine. Its rate is the cosine, but the cosine of what? Not of x. Of two point two, because that is the number actually arriving.
3. [20s] Multiply the rates, and check it -- Multiply them. Three, times the cosine of two point two, gives minus one point seven seven. That is the chain rule: the rate of the whole is the rate of the inside times the rate of the outside, taken where the inside lands. Measuring the combined function directly gives the same number.
4. [26s] The mistake everyone makes, and what it costs -- Here is the error worth seeing. Take the cosine of x rather than of u — cosine of nought point four rather than of two point two — and multiply by three. That gives plus two point seven six. Not slightly off: the wrong sign. The function is falling and the answer says it is rising, because the outer rate was read at the wrong place.
END

REQUEST
show arithmetic on a twelve-hour clock face, step around it by five and by four, and explain why one visits every position and the other only three

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [18s] Numbers that come back round -- A clock face with twelve positions. Counting past eleven does not give twelve — it gives zero, because the numbers come back round. This is not a convention anyone agreed to. It is what a circle does, and writing it down as remainders came afterwards.
2. [17s] Step by five, and visit everything -- Start at zero and keep adding five. Five, ten, then three, eight, one — the walk jumps around the face seemingly at random, but look at what it covers. Every single position, exactly once, before it returns to zero. Twelve steps, twelve positions.
3. [20s] Step by four, and most of the face is unreachable -- Now step by four instead. Four, eight, zero — and it is already back where it started, having touched three positions out of twelve. Nine of them can never be reached this way, no matter how long you keep adding four. Same clock, same kind of step, completely different reach.
4. [27s] The difference is a common factor -- What separates them is whether the step shares a factor with twelve. Five shares nothing with twelve, so it cannot settle into a short loop and has to visit everything. Four and twelve share a factor of four, and the walk closes after twelve divided by four — three steps. The reach is twelve over the greatest common divisor, and that holds for every step, not just these two.
END

REQUEST
show why a positive result on a very accurate medical test still means you are probably fine, by drawing ten thousand people as areas and counting the true and false positives

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [17s] A test that is right almost every time -- A disease that one person in a hundred has. A test that catches ninety-nine percent of the people who have it, and correctly clears ninety-five percent of those who do not. You take it. It comes back positive. How worried should you be?
2. [17s] Split the crowd by who is actually ill -- Take ten thousand people. One in a hundred means a hundred of them are ill — that thin sliver on the left. The other nine thousand nine hundred are not. Notice how small the sliver is. Everything that follows comes from that.
3. [25s] Now count everyone the test calls positive -- Run the test on all of them. Ninety-nine of the hundred ill people come back positive — the test is very good. But five percent of nine thousand nine hundred healthy people also come back positive, and five percent of a very large number is four hundred and ninety-five. Far more false alarms than real cases, from a test that is almost never wrong.
4. [26s] A positive result means one chance in six -- So of the five hundred and ninety-four people holding a positive result, only ninety-nine are actually ill. That is sixteen point seven percent — about one in six. The test did not lie and the arithmetic is not a trick. A small share of a very large group simply outnumbers most of a very small one, which is what the picture shows and what intuition refuses to.
END

REQUEST
play out the Monty Hall door problem, state the host's rule explicitly, explain why switching wins two times in three, and confirm it by simulating twenty thousand games

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [22s] Three doors, and the rules stated plainly -- Three doors. Behind one is a car, behind the other two, goats. You pick a door. Then — and this is the part every argument about this puzzle turns on — the host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the doors you did not pick, and always opens a goat. Should you switch?
2. [23s] Play one game, honestly -- Play it once. The car is behind a door chosen at random; you pick one; the host opens a goat door from what is left. Now there are two doors closed — the one you picked and one other. It looks like an even chance. It is not, and the reason is that the host's choice was not free.
3. [27s] Why the host's constraint moves the odds -- Think about your first pick. One time in three it was the car, and switching loses. Two times in three it was a goat — and then the host, forbidden from opening the car and forbidden from opening your door, has no choice at all. He must open the other goat, which leaves the car behind the door you switch to. Two cases out of three where switching wins.
4. [19s] Twenty thousand games settle it -- And if the argument still feels slippery, play it twenty thousand times. Switching wins sixty-six point three percent of them, staying wins thirty-three point seven, and those add to one — which is the check that the host was following his rule. Two thirds, counted rather than reasoned.
END

REQUEST
show Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor as cutting the largest possible squares off a rectangle until one fits exactly

  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [17s] A rectangle whose sides are the two numbers -- Two numbers: one thousand and seventy-one, and four hundred and sixty-two. What is the largest number that divides both? Draw them as a rectangle, that many units wide and that many tall. A common divisor is then a square that tiles the rectangle exactly.
2. [22s] Cut off as many squares as will fit -- Take the largest square that fits: four hundred and sixty-two on a side. Two of them fit along the length, and a strip is left over, one hundred and forty-seven wide. Any square that tiled the original must also tile that strip — so the problem has got smaller without the answer changing at all.
3. [19s] Repeat on what is left, until nothing is -- Now do the same to the strip. Squares of one hundred and forty-seven: three fit, and twenty-one is left. Squares of twenty-one: seven fit, and nothing is left over. That is the stopping point — the first square that tiles its rectangle exactly.
4. [17s] The last square is the answer -- Twenty-one. It divides both original numbers, and nothing larger does — which the scene confirms by testing every divisor up to the smaller number rather than taking Euclid's word for it. Three steps, where checking every candidate would have taken four hundred and sixty-two.
END

REQUEST
show binary search finding a number in a sorted list of sixty-four by halving the range each look, and compare the number of looks to checking one at a time

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [16s] Sixty-four numbers, sorted, and one to find -- Sixty-four numbers, in order, and one of them is the one we want. Checked one at a time from the left, the number forty-one is the forty-first thing you look at. Being sorted ought to be worth more than that.
2. [24s] Look in the middle, and throw half away -- Instead, look at the middle one. It is thirty-two, which is too small — so every number to its left is too small as well, and half the list is gone in a single look. Look at the middle of what remains. Too large this time, so the upper half goes. Each look costs one comparison and buys half the remaining list.
3. [15s] Found, and the count is the answer -- Forty-one, in six looks rather than forty-one. And six is not a coincidence: sixty-four halved six times is one. The number of looks is the number of halvings, which is the logarithm base two of the list length.
4. [20s] Why this scales and counting does not -- The difference matters most when the list is large. Double the numbers and one-at-a-time searching doubles its work, while halving needs exactly one more look. A million entries take twenty looks. A billion take thirty. That is what logarithmic means, and it is why sorted data is worth the trouble of sorting.
END

REQUEST
show the derivative as a limit of slopes — draw a secant line between two points on a curve, shrink the gap and show the computed slopes settling on a single value, then draw the tangent

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [20s] A curve, and one point on it -- A curve, and a point sitting on it. The question is how steep the curve is right there — not nearby, not on average, but at that exact point. Steepness is rise over run, and at a single point there is no run to divide by. That is the whole difficulty.
2. [22s] A second point gives a slope you can compute -- Put a second point on the curve, some distance along. Now there is a run, so there is a slope: the rise between them divided by the gap. That is a real number, and it is not the answer — it is the average steepness across the whole stretch, which is not what was asked.
3. [22s] Shrink the gap and watch the number settle -- Now close the gap. The second point slides towards the first and the slope changes as it goes — but it does not wander. It settles. One point one four, then nought point four five, then closer and closer to a single value it never quite reaches, because reaching it would mean dividing by zero.
4. [22s] The value it settles on is the derivative -- That settling value is the derivative. Here it is minus zero point two five, and the line through the point with that slope is the tangent — the straight line that matches the curve's direction exactly. The formula gives the same number at every point, which is checked against the slopes themselves before it is written down.
END

Follow the same seven-term polynomial out past five and it does not track sine at all — it dives away and never comes back. The approximation is local. It is built entirely from what sine does at zero, and far enough from zero that information runs out. Adding terms widens the good stretch; it does not make it everything.

REQUEST
approximate the sine curve with polynomials, adding one term at a time and showing the error shrink near the centre, then show the same polynomial diverging far from it

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [18s] A curve, and a straight line that matches it at one point -- Here is the sine curve. Suppose all you are allowed is a polynomial — additions and multiplications, nothing else. How close can you get? Start with the simplest thing that touches the curve at zero and leaves in the same direction: the line y equals x.
2. [20s] Each extra term fixes the next derivative -- Add a term chosen so the polynomial's second derivative matches too, then its third, then its fourth. Each new coefficient is the matching derivative of sine at zero, divided by that many factorial — computed, not looked up. Watch the approximation grip the curve over a wider and wider stretch each time.
3. [22s] Near the centre, the error collapses -- Measure it. At x equals one point four, the straight line is out by more than four tenths. Three terms brings that down to four hundredths, five terms to two thousandths, seven terms to six parts in a hundred thousand. Each term really does help — and the scene checks that it does before saying so.
4. [29s] Far from the centre, it falls apart -- But more terms is not always better, and this is where most explanations stop too early. Follow the same seven-term polynomial out past five and it does not track sine at all — it dives away and never comes back. The approximation is local. It is built entirely from what sine does at zero, and far enough from zero that information runs out. Adding terms widens the good stretch; it does not make it everything.
END

REQUEST
prove Pythagoras by rearrangement — pack four copies of the same right triangle into a square two different ways and show the leftover areas must be equal

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [21s] One right triangle, and the squares on its sides -- A right triangle, with legs of five and twelve. Build a square on each of the three sides. The claim to be proved is that the two smaller squares, added together, come to exactly the same area as the big one — and that this holds for every right triangle, not just this one.
2. [20s] Four copies, packed into a square, one way -- Take four identical copies of the triangle and a square whose side is the two legs added together. Pack the four into two opposite corners. What is left is two squares — one with side a, one with side b. Nothing has been computed yet; the pieces were simply put somewhere.
3. [18s] The same four, packed the other way -- Now the same square, and the same four triangles, turned into a pinwheel around the edges. Every piece is identical to before and the outer square is identical to before. What is left this time is a single tilted square, and its side is the hypotenuse.
4. [24s] Same square, same pieces, so the leftovers match -- Both outer squares have the same area. Both contain the same four triangles. So whatever is left must be equal — and that is the proof. The two small squares on the legs and the one tilted square on the hypotenuse are the same area, here and for every right triangle, because nothing in the argument used the particular numbers.
END

REQUEST
show why the area of a circle is pi r squared by cutting it into wedges and interleaving them into a rectangle, and show the approximation improving as the wedges get thinner

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [19s] A disc, and the number we want -- A disc of radius r. Everyone knows its area is pi r squared, and almost nobody is shown why. The argument is a rearrangement: cut the disc into wedges and lay them out differently, without losing or gaining any area, until the shape is one whose area is obvious.
2. [20s] Cut it into wedges and interleave them -- Cut the disc into eight equal wedges and lay them out in a row, alternating point up and point down so they interlock. Not one scrap of area has been added or removed — the same eight pieces are simply somewhere else. The shape they make is nearly a parallelogram.
3. [27s] The shape is short, and by how much -- Here is the part usually skipped. The width really is pi r — half the circumference, laid end to end. But the height is not r. It is r times the cosine of pi over n, because each wedge is a triangle with a curved top, and for eight wedges that is about nine tenths of r. The rearranged shape falls short of pi r squared, and it should.
4. [25s] Thinner wedges, and the shortfall vanishes -- Now use more wedges. Sixteen, then thirty-two. The zig-zag along the top flattens, the height climbs towards r, and the shortfall falls away — under two percent, then under half a percent. In the limit the shape is exactly a rectangle, pi r wide and r high, and its area is pi r squared. That is the formula, and that is where it comes from.
END

REQUEST
show a covalent bond forming as two hydrogen atoms come together, plot the energy against their separation, and show that the bond is the bottom of that curve

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [15s] Two atoms, far apart, ignoring each other -- Two hydrogen atoms, a long way apart. Neither one feels the other, so there is nothing to gain by moving and nothing to lose. Call that energy zero — it is the reference everything else is measured against.
2. [17s] Bringing them closer releases energy -- Now push them together. Each electron starts to feel both nuclei at once, and being pulled from two sides is a lower-energy place to be than being pulled from one. The curve falls. The atoms are not being forced together — they are falling.
3. [18s] Pushing further costs more than it gains -- Keep pushing and the curve turns around. The two nuclei are both positive, and at close range that repulsion beats everything else. So there is a distance that is better than being apart and better than being closer — and that is what a bond is.
4. [18s] The bottom of the curve is the bond -- The lowest point sits at seventy-four picometres apart, four hundred and thirty-six kilojoules per mole below where the atoms started. That depth is the bond: supply that much energy and the two atoms climb back out and go their separate ways. Supply less, and they stay.
END

2. [17s] Run it, and watch them go -- Run the clock. Early on a great many react, simply because there are a great many left to react. Later, fewer and fewer go — not because any particle has become less likely to react, but because there are fewer of them to try.

4. [20s] The half-life is the same wherever you start -- One number describes the whole curve. The half-life: the time for half of whatever is present to go. REQUEST
show a reaction as individual particles reacting at random, then plot the concentration falling and show it follows an exponential with a fixed half-life

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [15s] A box of particles, each with the same chance -- A box of reactant. Every particle in it is identical, and on any given moment each one has the same small chance of reacting — independent of the others, and independent of how long it has already been waiting.
2. [17s] Run it, and watch them go -- Run the clock. Early on a great many react, simply because there are a great many left to react. Later, fewer and fewer go — not because any particle has become less likely to react, but because there are fewer of them to try.
3. [19s] Plot the count against time -- Plot what just happened. The points are the counts from the simulation — nothing smoothed, nothing fitted. The curve over them is the prediction: the starting amount times e to the minus k t. They lie on top of each other, which is the claim being made good.
4. [20s] The half-life is the same wherever you start -- One number describes the whole curve. The half-life: the time for half of whatever is present to go. From a hundred and fifty down to seventy-five takes the same time as seventy-five down to thirty-seven — and the same again after that. It is log two over k, and it never changes.
END

REQUEST
show breadth-first search expanding outward from a node in waves, and show that it finds the shortest path when every edge costs one

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [17s] A graph, and a place to start -- A network: things, and which of them are connected. We start at A and want to reach everything else. The only question is what order to look in — and the order turns out to decide what the search is good for.
2. [19s] Everything one step away, then everything two -- Breadth-first means exactly what it says: finish the whole of one ring before starting the next. Everything one step from A. Then everything two steps away. Then three. The search grows as a wave rather than a thread, and no node is ever reached before its turn.
3. [19s] The depth it was found at is the distance -- Here is what the wave bought us. Because rings are finished in order, the ring a node was found in is the fewest steps from the start to it. Not an estimate — the answer. When every edge costs the same, breadth-first search solves the shortest-path problem for free.
4. [17s] Follow the links back to get the route -- And the route itself is already recorded. Each node remembers which neighbour reached it first, so walking those links backwards from any node returns the shortest path to it. From I back to A: four steps, and there is no shorter way.
END

REQUEST
show Dijkstra's algorithm relaxing edges and settling on the cheapest route, on a graph where the route with fewest steps is not the cheapest, and explain why the greedy choice is safe

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [19s] The same network, but the edges cost different amounts -- The same kind of network, with one change: crossing an edge now costs something, and the costs differ. Counting steps no longer answers the question. Look at A and D. There is a single edge between them — one step, the fewest possible — and taking it costs fourteen.
2. [24s] Keep a running estimate, and improve it -- Give every node a running estimate of the cheapest way to reach it: zero for A, unknown for the rest. Then take the cheapest node not yet finished, and look at what it leads to. If going through it beats a node's current estimate, lower the estimate. Watch D. It starts at fourteen, drops to eleven, and finally to nine.
3. [29s] Why settling the cheapest one is safe -- The greedy step looks reckless: once a node is settled its estimate is never revisited. It is safe because of the order. Any other route to that node has to leave through some node that is still unsettled, and every one of those already costs at least as much — so the detour cannot come back cheaper. That argument needs every cost to be positive, and it fails the moment one is not.
4. [22s] The answer, checked against every route -- The cheapest way from A to D costs nine, and it takes three steps rather than one. Before saying that, the scene enumerates every route through this network and confirms there is nothing cheaper. Greedy algorithms are exactly the ones that look right while being wrong on a case the drawing happens not to contain.
END

REQUEST
colour a graph so no two connected nodes match, show that the greedy method's answer depends on the order you take the nodes in, and compare it to the true minimum

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [20s] Colour the nodes so no edge joins two the same -- A network, and one rule: give every node a colour so that no edge ever joins two nodes of the same colour. This is timetabling in disguise — the nodes are exams, the edges are students sitting both, and the colours are time slots. Fewer colours means a shorter exam period.
2. [20s] The obvious method: take the lowest colour that fits -- The obvious method is to go through the nodes one at a time and give each the lowest-numbered colour none of its neighbours has yet. It is fast, it never breaks the rule, and here it finishes in two colours. Left side green, right side amber, and every edge crosses between them.
3. [22s] Same graph, same method, a different order -- Now change nothing except the order. Take one node from the left, then one from the right, and alternate. The rule is applied exactly as before and the answer is still valid — but it uses three colours instead of two. The graph did not change. The algorithm did not change. Only the order did.
4. [26s] Knowing the true minimum means searching for it -- So which is right? Two is, and finding that out took a search through every way of colouring the graph — hundreds of assignments for six nodes, and rising as a power of the number of nodes. That is the real shape of the difficulty. A valid colouring is easy and a good one is usually easy. Being certain you cannot do better is what costs.
END

REQUEST
show the seven bridges of Konigsberg, try and fail to cross each exactly once, then prove it is impossible by counting how many bridges touch each piece of land

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [17s] Four pieces of land, seven bridges -- Konigsberg, seventeen thirty-six. A river splits the city into four pieces: two banks, an island, and a quarter to the east. Seven bridges join them. The townspeople asked a question that sounds like a puzzle and turned out to start a branch of mathematics.
2. [27s] The question, and three honest attempts -- Can you walk through the city crossing every bridge exactly once? Try it. Start on the north bank and you strand yourself with a bridge still unused. Start on the island instead — stranded again. Start in the east quarter and you barely get going. Something is always left over, and no amount of trying tells you whether you are unlucky or whether it cannot be done at all.
3. [26s] Throw the map away and keep the connections -- Euler's move was to stop looking at the map. The shape of the island does not matter, nor the length of any bridge, nor which way the river bends. The only thing that decides the answer is which pieces of land are joined, and by how many bridges. Shrink each piece of land to a dot and the whole problem is four dots and seven lines.
4. [29s] Count the odd ones, and the answer is forced -- Here is the argument. Any piece of land you pass through costs two bridges — one to arrive, one to leave. So a land touched by an odd number of bridges can only be where you start or where you finish. A walk has two ends. But every one of these four is odd: five, three, three, three. Four candidates for two positions. The walk does not exist, and no cleverness will find it.
END

3. [12s] Double the count and watch the gap close -- Now use more, thinner rectangles. Four. Eight. Sixteen. Thirty-two. Each time the count doubles, the gap left over is cut roughly in half — and the total climbs steadily toward something.

END

show the law of large numbers with coin flips — start with ten flips landing far from a half, then keep flipping and show the proportion wandering in toward it, and show that the error shrinks like one over root n

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

1. [14s] Flip a coin ten times and look at the proportion -- Flip a fair coin ten times. You might expect five heads. This run gave seven — a proportion of zero point seven, nowhere near a half. Small samples are not gently wrong. They are wildly wrong.
2. [16s] Keep flipping and watch it wander inward -- Keep going. It does not march politely to a half — it wanders, overshooting and correcting. But the wandering gets smaller. Not because later flips correct earlier ones, but because each new flip counts for less against a growing total.
3. [19s] The wander shrinks like one over root n -- And the shrinking has a shape. The typical distance from a half falls like one over the square root of the number of flips — so to halve your error you need four times the data. That is why polls are expensive, and why they are never quite certain.
END

This equation represents the position of the object as it oscillates back and forth.

The variable A represents the amplitude of the motion, which is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position. 7. [28s] Prime number theorem. -- One of the most fascinating aspects of prime numbers is the Prime Number Theorem, which provides an approximation for the distribution of prime numbers. The theorem states that the number of primes less than a given number n is approximately n divided by the natural logarithm of n. This theorem helps mathematicians understand the density of prime numbers and makes predictions about their occurrence. While the theorem is a powerful tool, it's important to note that it's an approximation and not an exact formula.
8. [24s] Twin prime conjecture. -- Another intriguing topic in the study of prime numbers is the Twin Prime Conjecture. This conjecture suggests that there are infinitely many pairs of prime numbers that differ by 2, such as (3, 5), (5, 7), and (11, 13). Despite extensive research, the Twin Prime Conjecture remains unproven, and it continues to challenge mathematicians to find a solution. The conjecture highlights the ongoing nature of mathematical exploration and the pursuit of new knowledge.
9. [26s] Mersenne primes. -- Mersenne primes are a special subset of prime numbers that are one less than a power of two. These primes are named after the French mathematician Marin Mersenne, who studied their properties in the 17th century. Mersenne primes have unique characteristics and have been the subject of extensive research due to their significance in number theory and computer science. The largest known Mersenne primes are discovered using sophisticated algorithms and computer programs, showcasing the intersection of mathematics and technology.

[27s] Goldbach's conjecture. -- Another famous unsolved problem in mathematics is Goldbach's Conjecture, which states that every even integer greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two prime numbers. For example, the number 8 can be written as the sum of the primes 3 and 5. Despite its simplicity, Goldbach's Conjecture has eluded proof for over 250 years, and it continues to captivate mathematicians with its elegance and challenge. The conjecture serves as a reminder of the depth and complexity of mathematical problems.
11. [26s] Sieve of Eratosthenes. -- To find prime numbers efficiently, mathematicians have developed various algorithms and methods. One such method is the Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a specified integer. The Sieve of Eratosthenes works by iteratively marking the multiples of each prime number starting from 2. The remaining unmarked numbers are identified as prime numbers. This algorithm is a testament to the power of mathematical reasoning and its ability to solve complex problems with elegance.
12. [24s] Distribution of prime numbers. -- The distribution of prime numbers is a fascinating topic that has been studied for centuries. These tools help researchers understand the density of prime numbers and make predictions about their occurrence. The study of prime number distribution continues to be an active area of research in number theory.

1. [20s] Wave equation on screen. -- This is the standard wave equation for a field u. It describes how a wave propagates through a medium. The equation is partial derivative squared u with respect to t squared equals c squared times partial derivative squared u with respect to x squared. This is a fundamental equation in physics and mathematics, governing the behavior of waves in various contexts.
2. [16s] Highlighting c. -- Now, let's focus on the variable c in the equation. c represents the speed of wave propagation. It's a crucial parameter that determines how fast the wave travels through the medium. The value of c depends on the properties of the medium, such as its density and elasticity.
3. [11s] Transition to sinusoidal solutions. -- Solutions to the wave equation typically involve sinusoidal functions. These functions are periodic and oscillatory, making them ideal for describing waves. The most common sinusoidal functions used in solutions are sine and cosine functions.
4. [22s] Cosine solution example. -- Here's an example of a solution to the wave equation using the cosine function. u(x, t) equals A times cosine of kx minus ωt. This represents a wave propagating in the positive x-direction. The amplitude A determines the height of the wave, the wavenumber k relates to the wavelength of the wave, and the angular frequency ω is related to the period of the wave.
5. [11s] Explanation of A. -- The symbol A in the equation represents the amplitude of the wave. Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the wave from its equilibrium position. It's a measure of the wave's energy and intensity.
6. [11s] Explanation of k. -- The symbol k stands for the wavenumber. Wavenumber is the spatial frequency of the wave, which is the number of wave cycles per unit distance. It's inversely related to the wavelength of the wave.

I would like to create an educational animation that demonstrates the process of calculating a definite integral. Specifically, it should show the integration of x cubed from 0 to 2. The animation should begin by presenting the integration problem, then explain how to apply the power rule for definite integration. Next, it should show the step-by-step process of integrating x cubed, starting with the application of the power rule and finishing with the evaluation of the integral at the boundaries 0 and 2. Finally, the animation should conclude by clearly showing the numeric solution to the integral. Can you create an animation like this for a classroom setting that helps students understand the concept visually?

This means that the area under the curve of x cubed from 0 to 2 is exactly 3.75 square units. Well, it's a way to integrate a function over a surface in three-dimensional space. It's like a double integral, but instead of integrating over an area in a plane, we're integrating over a surface in space."

The sphere has a radius, say, of 'a'. Our goal is to find the surface integral of the function f(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 over the entire surface of this sphere. To do this, we need to parameterize the surface of the sphere. That means we need to find a way to describe every point on the sphere using two parameters."
3. [33s] Spherical coordinates explained. -- "Now, you might already be familiar with spherical coordinates. In spherical coordinates, we describe a point in space using three numbers: the radius 'r', the polar angle 'θ', and the azimuthal angle 'φ'. The radius 'r' is the distance from the origin to the point, 'θ' is the angle between the positive z-axis and the line from the origin to the point, and 'φ' is the angle between the positive x-axis and the projection of the line from the origin to the point onto the xy-plane. For a sphere centered at the origin, 'r' is constant and equal to 'a'."
4. [28s] Parameterization of the sphere. -- "So, to parameterize the sphere, we can use spherical coordinates. We can write the position vector r as a function of 'θ' and 'φ'. The x, y, and z coordinates of a point on the sphere can be written in terms of 'θ' and 'φ' as follows: x = a sinθ cosφ, y = a sinθ sinφ, and z = a cosθ. This gives us a parameterization of the sphere, where 'θ' ranges from 0 to π, and 'φ' ranges from 0 to 2π."

6. [24s] Partial derivatives of r. -- "So, let's find the partial derivatives of r with respect to 'θ' and 'φ'. The position vector r is given by r(θ, φ) = (a sinθ cosφ, a sinθ sinφ, a cosθ). Well, a Fourier Series is a way to represent a periodic function using an infinite sum of sines and cosines. It's named after Joseph Fourier, a French mathematician who lived in the early 1800s. He was the first to propose that any periodic function could be represented in this way."

1. [15s] Draw a spring-mass-damper system -- Here is a spring-mass-damper system. A mass, m, is attached to a spring with spring constant k. A damper, with damping coefficient c, is also attached to the mass. This system is subject to an external force, F(t), and experiences displacement, x(t), from its equilibrium position.
2. [16s] Write down the equation of motion -- The equation of motion for this system is given by Newton's second law, F(t) = m * a(t), where a(t) is the acceleration. The acceleration is the second derivative of displacement with respect to time, a(t) = d²x/dt². So, the equation becomes F(t) = m * d²x/dt².
3. [11s] Introduce the spring force -- The spring exerts a force proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, F_spring = -k * x(t). This is Hooke's law. So, the equation becomes F(t) = m * d²x/dt² + k * x(t).
4. [12s] Introduce the damping force -- The damper exerts a force proportional to the velocity, F_damper = -c * dx/dt. This is Stokes' law. So, the equation becomes F(t) = m * d²x/dt² + c * dx/dt + k * x(t).
5. [12s] Rewrite the equation in standard form -- To make it easier to solve, we can rewrite the equation in standard form. Divide both sides by m, and rearrange the terms to get d²x/dt² + (c/m) * dx/dt + (k/m) * x(t) = F(t)/m.
6. [16s] Introduce the characteristic equation -- For free vibration (F(t) = 0), the equation becomes d²x/dt² + (c/m) * dx/dt + (k/m) * x(t) = 0. This is a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients. The solution to this equation is of the form x(t) = e^(rt), where r is a constant.

1. [25s] Derive the wave equation -- Imagine a string stretched tight between two fixed points. Now, imagine plucking it and letting it vibrate. The wave equation describes how the string moves over time. We start with Newton's second law, F = ma, and Hooke's law, F = -kx. Combining these, we get the wave equation: ∂²u/∂t² = c²∂²u/∂x², where u is the displacement of the string, c is the wave speed, and x and t are spatial and temporal coordinates.
2. [23s] General solution form -- The wave equation is a second-order linear partial differential equation. Its general solution is u(x,t) = f(x-ct) + g(x+ct), where f and g are arbitrary functions determined by the initial conditions of the string. This means any solution can be expressed as the sum of two waves traveling in opposite directions. The shape of the string at any time is the sum of the shapes of these two waves.
3. [21s] Initial conditions -- To find the specific functions f and g, we need initial conditions. These are the shape of the string at t=0, u(x,0) = φ(x), and its derivative with respect to time at t=0, ∂u/∂t(x,0) = ψ(x). Using these, we can express f and g in terms of φ and ψ. This shows how the initial conditions determine the future behavior of the string.
4. [19s] Visualize the solution -- Let's visualize the general solution. Imagine the string at t=0. Now, imagine two identical strings, one moving to the right and one to the left. The sum of these two strings gives the shape of the original string at any later time. The right-moving string is determined by f, and the left-moving string is determined by g.
5. [20s] Special case: standing waves -- A special case of the wave equation is the standing wave. This occurs when the initial conditions are such that the string's motion is periodic and doesn't travel. The general solution for a standing wave is u(x,t) = f(x)cos(ωt), where ω is the angular frequency. This is a solution where the string oscillates in place, with nodes and antinodes.
6. [17s] d'Alembert's formula -- Now, let's consider d'Alembert's formula. This is a special solution to the wave equation for a semi-infinite string with a fixed endpoint. It's given by u(x,t) = φ(x-ct) + ψ(x+ct)/c, where φ and ψ are the initial displacement and velocity. This formula shows how the initial conditions propagate along the string.

The negative sign indicates that the force is always directed towards the equilibrium position, opposing the displacement.

Here, x represents the displacement of the mass from its equilibrium position. The second derivative of x with respect to time, d²x/dt², represents the acceleration of the mass. The term (k/m) is the square of the natural frequency of the system, where k is the spring constant and m is the mass. This term determines the rate at which the system oscillates.

1. [21s] Mass-spring system diagram. -- Welcome to this educational animation on harmonic oscillators. Today, we'll explore the physics behind a mass-spring system. Imagine a mass attached to a spring, which is in turn attached to a wall. When the mass is displaced from its equilibrium position, the spring exerts a restoring force, causing the mass to oscillate back and forth. This is the essence of a harmonic oscillator.
2. [29s] Equation of motion: F = -kx = ma. -- The equation of motion for this system is given by Hooke's Law, which states that the force exerted by the spring is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium. This can be written as F = -kx, where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement. According to Newton's second law, F = ma, where m is the mass and a is the acceleration. Combining these two equations, we get the second-order ordinary differential equation ma = -kx, which describes the motion of the mass-spring system.
3. [22s] Equation of motion: x'' + (k/m)x = 0. -- To simplify this equation, we can divide both sides by m and rewrite it in terms of the second derivative of x with respect to time. This gives us the standard form of the harmonic oscillator equation: x'' + (k/m)x = 0. Here, x'' represents the second derivative of x with respect to time. This equation is a second-order linear ordinary differential equation with constant coefficients.
4. [22s] Characteristic equation: r^2 + (k/m) = 0. -- To solve this differential equation, we can use the method of undetermined coefficients. We assume a solution of the form x(t) = e^(rt), where r is a constant. Substituting this into the differential equation, we obtain the characteristic equation: r^2 + (k/m) = 0. This is a quadratic equation in r, and its solutions will determine the nature of the motion of the mass-spring system.
5. [18s] Roots of characteristic equation: r = ±i√(k/m). -- The roots of the characteristic equation are given by r = ±i√(k/m). Here, i represents the imaginary unit, and √(k/m) is the natural frequency of the oscillator. The presence of imaginary roots indicates that the solution will be oscillatory in nature. The natural frequency determines the rate at which the mass oscillates back and forth.
6. [23s] General solution: x(t) = A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt). -- The general solution to the differential equation is a linear combination of the two fundamental solutions corresponding to the roots of the characteristic equation. This gives us the general solution: x(t) = A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt). Here, ω represents the angular frequency, which is related to the natural frequency by ω = √(k/m). The constants A and B are determined by the initial conditions of the system.

13. [21s] Gibbs Phenomenon -- However, it's important to note that adding more terms doesn't always improve the approximation near sharp corners and discontinuities. This is known as the Gibbs phenomenon. In these regions, the approximation may exhibit oscillations that don't decrease in amplitude as we add more terms. This is a limitation of Fourier series and something to keep in mind when using them to approximate functions.
14. [17s] Applications of Fourier Series -- Now that we've seen how Fourier series can be used to approximate functions, let's discuss some of their applications. Fourier series are widely used in signal processing, where they can be used to analyze and manipulate signals. They're also used in solving differential equations, particularly those with periodic boundary conditions.
15. [16s] Discrete Fourier Transform -- Another important application of Fourier series is the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). The DFT is a numerical algorithm that computes the Fourier coefficients of a discrete set of data points. It's used in various fields, including image and audio processing, to analyze and manipulate signals in the frequency domain.
16. [18s] Fast Fourier Transform -- The fast Fourier transform (FFT) is an efficient algorithm for computing the DFT. It reduces the number of computations required from O(N²) to O(N log N), making it much faster and more practical for large datasets. The FFT is widely used in various applications, from image and audio processing to radar and wireless communications.
17. [19s] Conclusion -- In conclusion, Fourier series are a powerful mathematical tool for approximating periodic functions using simple trigonometric functions. They have numerous applications in various fields, from signal processing to solving differential equations. By adding more terms to the series, we can achieve increasingly accurate approximations, although there are some limitations, such as the Gibbs phenomenon, to keep in mind.
18. [22s] Fading Out -- As we fade everything out, remember that Fourier series are a fundamental concept in mathematics and have wide-ranging applications. Thank you for joining us in this Fourier Series Demo, and we hope you've gained a better understanding of this important mathematical tool.
